title: Chicken as food
description: Most popular and affordable source of high-quality protein
wiki_lead:
Chicken is the most common type of poultry and the second most consumed meat in the world, after pork. Owing to the relative ease and low cost of raising chickens—in comparison to mammals such as cattle or pigs—chicken meat (commonly called just "chicken") and chicken eggs have become prevalent in numerous cuisines.
Chicken can be prepared in a vast range of ways, including baking, grilling, barbecuing, frying, boiling, and roasting. Since the latter half of the 20th century, prepared chicken has become a staple of fast food. Chicken is sometimes cited as being more healthy than red meat, with lower concentrations of cholesterol and saturated fat.
The poultry farming industry that accounts for chicken production takes on a range of forms across different parts of the world. In developed countries, chickens are typically subject to intensive farming methods while less-developed areas raise chickens using more traditional farming techniques. The United Nations estimated there to be 19 billion chickens on Earth in 2011, making them outnumber humans more than two to one. Chickens are recognized as sentient animals capable of experiencing pain and distress, which has led to ongoing scientific and ethical discussions regarding their treatment in food production systems.

The United Nations estimated there to be 19 billion chickens on Earth in 2011, making them outnumber humans more than two to one. Chickens are recognized as sentient animals capable of experiencing pain and distress, which has led to ongoing scientific and ethical discussions regarding their treatment in food production systems.


History

The modern chicken is a descendant of red junglefowl hybrids along with the grey junglefowl first raised thousands of years ago in the northern parts of the Indian subcontinent.
Chicken as a meat has been depicted in Babylonian carvings from around 600 BC. Chicken was one of the most common meats available in the Middle Ages. For thousands of years, a number of different kinds of chicken have been eaten across most of the Eastern Hemisphere, including capons, pullets, and hens. It was one of the basic ingredients in blancmange, a stew usually consisting of chicken and fried onions cooked in milk and seasoned with spices and sugar.
In the United States in the 1800s, chicken was more expensive than other meats and it was "sought by the rich because [it is] so costly as to be an uncommon dish." Chicken consumption in the U.S. increased during World War II due to a shortage of beef and pork. 
In the post-World War II period, the USDA along with the A&P and others embarked on a program to breed the chicken of tomorrow. The techniques of Robert Bakewell (agriculturist) were employed.  This led to the creation of the Cornish Rock Cross in the late 1940s - a chicken with an efficient feed conversion ratio (FCR), speedy to rear, and good meat quality.  A documentary The Chicken of Tomorrow was made.  The trends for improved FCR and quality have continued, and the adoption of this higher-yielding chickens spread from USA to Europe and beyond.  The trend for improvements in efficiency has continued since then, alongside changes in animal welfare.
In Europe, consumption of chicken overtook that of beef and veal in 1996, linked to consumer awareness of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (mad cow disease).
357 million tonnes of meat were produced in 2021, 53% more than in 2000, with chicken meat representing more than half the increase. Chicken meat was the most produced type of meat in 2021 just ahead of pig meat. Fast-growing breeds such as the Cobb 500 and Ross 308 are used in mass agricultural production of meat chicken.  Some countries are moving towards some slower-growing breeds, such as the Hubbard JA787, or introducing standards for higher welfare.


Breeding

Modern varieties of chicken such as the Cornish Cross, are bred specifically for meat production, with an emphasis placed on the ratio of feed to meat produced by the animal. The most common breeds of chicken consumed in the U.S. are Cornish and White Rock.
Chickens raised specifically for food are called broilers. In the U.S., broilers are typically butchered at a young age. Modern Cornish Cross hybrids, for example, are butchered as early as 8 weeks for fryers and 12 weeks for roasting birds.

grok_lead: Chicken as food refers to the meat obtained from domesticated chickens ( Gallus gallus domesticus), a staple animal protein consumed worldwide for its affordability, nutritional value, and adaptability in diverse cuisines. Domesticated initially around 1650â1250 BCE in Southeast Asia, chickens have been selectively bred over millennia for rapid growth and high meat yield, making broiler production one of the most efficient forms of livestock farming. In 2023, global poultry meat production reached approximately 146 million tonnes, with chicken comprising the majority, underscoring its dominance in the meat sector due to short rearing cycles of 6â8 weeks and feed conversion efficiencies superior to other meats. Nutritionally, chicken meat is a complete protein source containing all essential amino acids, with skinless breast providing about 31 grams of protein per 100 grams while being relatively low in saturated fat compared to beef or pork, contributing to its popularity in health-conscious diets. Per capita poultry consumption averages around 15 kilograms annually worldwide, though it varies significantly, with high-income countries like the United States exceeding 50 kilograms due to abundant supply and cultural preferences for processed forms such as nuggets and wings. Economically, the industry generates hundreds of billions in value, supporting millions of jobs through integrated supply chains from breeding to processing, though it faces challenges like disease outbreaks and environmental concerns from large-scale operations. While cooked skinless chicken breast provides about 31 grams of protein and 165 calories per 100 grams (approximately 1,650 calories per kilogram), raw boneless skinless chicken breast contains approximately 23 grams of protein and 120 calories per 100 grams (1,200 calories per kilogram) (USDA data). This difference arises from moisture loss during cooking, which concentrates the nutrients. Raw values are relevant for portion planning when purchasing uncooked meat.
